source.title: Lazy vs hasty: linearization in deep networks impacts learning schedule based on example difficulty
source.authors: Thomas George; Guillaume Lajoie; A. Baratin

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares feature learning with linearized training and measures learning dynamics and test loss on natural, noisy-label, and spurious-correlation tasks; this is related conceptual evidence about generalization, but it does not test the claim's memorization-capacity comparison.
record.gate_note: The study reports learning curves and relative test-loss or accuracy results for the α-scaled regimes. Linearity metrics are used to verify the regimes; record the reported feature-learning and test-outcome comparisons, not the metrics used only to verify linearity.
record.test_reason: The study compares feature-learning and linearized training through example-difficulty learning curves and test performance. None of its interventions measures V1–V8. In particular, corrupting 15% of CIFAR-10 labels measures selective memorization dynamics, not V1's comparison of fitting fully randomized versus natural labels and their held-out accuracy. The record's tests/T2 classification should be corrected.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: compared with linearized training, feature learning gives easier examples greater early priority across C-scores, label noise and spurious correlations. A tractable quadratic model illustrates this learning schedule. This preference can help with label noise but hurt early robustness to spurious correlations.
record.recipe_differences: The study modulates linearity through α scaling and compares nonlinear feature learning with a linearized regime. It measures relative learning schedules and some test outcomes, not the original study's memorization/generalization interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative advantage changes with task and training phase: linearized training does better on non-spurious examples early in the CelebA and Waterbirds experiments, while nonlinear training has a slight advantage later on Waterbirds. The noisy-label comparison is made at equal clean-example loss; the C-score comparison is normalized by mean training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched mean training loss, feature-learning networks prioritize high-C-score examples more strongly than linearized networks (Section 3.2.1; Figures 2, 9–11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning amplifies the relative learning-speed advantage of easier examples compared with linearized training.

fits_no_version.finding: With 15% corrupted CIFAR-10 training labels, feature learning delays noisy-label memorization at matched clean-example progress and achieves better peak test performance (Section 3.2.2; Figures 2, 8 and 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compared with linearized training, feature learning can prioritize clean examples and improve peak generalization under partial label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: On CelebA and Waterbirds, linearized training initially gives higher test accuracy and learns examples lacking the spurious correlation comparatively faster; later results converge, with a slight nonlinear advantage on Waterbirds (Section 3.3; Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature learning's early preference for easy examples can increase susceptibility to spurious correlations, with phase-dependent generalization consequences.

record.problems: The results concern learning schedules and selected test-loss or accuracy trajectories, not the catalog claim's random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence. Many findings are shown in figures without exact extracted numeric values; experiments use selected datasets and architectures, and some comparisons are phase-dependent.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The study's reported results concern example-difficulty learning schedules and selected test metrics, which do not measure the behavior named by any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels versus natural labels under the same recipe, with above-chance natural-label and chance random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout's effect on held-out error and its dependence on training-set size, strength, or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The empty result-row set is appropriate for V1–V8. The related findings are already declared in rows_left_out, so they do not require missing entries. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test fitting fixed random labels versus natural labels, chance test accuracy on random labels, or the listed Zhang et al. architectures.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures for test error.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
